summary.text: A star is a luminous ball of plasma held together by its own gravity, and the one nearest to Earth is the Sun.
A star's life begins when a gas cloud of mostly hydrogen and helium collapses under gravity, and its total mass mainly decides how it evolves and ends.
For most of its active life a star shines by fusing hydrogen into helium in its core, and when fusion stops the core becomes a white dwarf, a neutron star or a black hole.

facts.label: Visible by eye
facts.value: About 4,000 stars, all in the Milky Way

facts.label: What powers it
facts.value: Fusion of hydrogen into helium in its core

facts.label: Heavy elements
facts.value: Stars create almost all elements heavier than lithium

facts.label: Possible remnants
facts.value: White dwarf, neutron star or black hole

items.prompt: On a clear night, nearly every star you can see looks like a tiny, steady dot, never a visible disc. What best explains that?

options.label: Stars are much smaller than the planets beside them
They are so far from Earth that they shrink to points of light
They only reflect light, so each shows as a faint dot
They are fixed to a sphere that hides their true size

items.explain: The immense distances of stars from Earth make them appear as fixed points of light.

items.prompt: Two newborn stars form from similar clouds of gas, but one ends up with much more total mass. What does that difference mainly settle?

options.label: How each star evolves and how it eventually ends
Which constellation each star is grouped into
How many planets will orbit each star
What name astronomers will give each star

items.explain: A star's total mass mainly determines its evolution and eventual fate.

items.prompt: A friend says the Sun shines because it burns, like a giant bonfire. What actually powers a star through most of its active life?

options.label: Chemical burning of gas in its outer layers
Light reflected from other stars nearby
Fusion of hydrogen into helium in its core
Friction from planets moving through it

items.explain: A star shines for most of its active life because hydrogen fuses into helium in its core, releasing energy that radiates into space.

items.prompt: A very heavy star's core stops fusing for good. Which fate can await it?

options.label: It becomes a planet circling a younger star
It restarts as a fresh cloud of hydrogen gas
It turns into a brighter star with new fuel
It can become a black hole

items.explain: When fusion ceases, the core becomes a stellar remnant, and a sufficiently massive star leaves a black hole.

items.prompt: A dying star throws off material rich in heavy elements. How can that material end up in a later star?

options.label: It returns to the space between stars and is recycled into new stars
It sinks back into the old core, where it stays locked away
It is destroyed, so later stars hold only hydrogen and helium
It escapes as pure light, so nothing is ever reused

items.explain: Mass loss or supernova explosions return enriched material to the interstellar medium, and those elements are then recycled into new stars.

items.prompt: Ancient sky-watchers sorted the lights above into two kinds by how they moved. Which description fits the "wandering stars"?

options.label: Lights that blink on and off from one night to the next
Lights that shift noticeably against the rest over days or weeks
Lights that appear only during a lunar eclipse
Lights that brighten and fade on a yearly cycle

items.explain: Wandering stars moved noticeably relative to the fixed stars over days or weeks.
